segments.text: Rubbery whites, a grey ring around the yolk, shells that will not come off:
boiled eggs go wrong in so many ways, and today I will fix all
of them.
You need eggs, a pot, a timer, and a bowl of ice water.
That is it.
Bring a pot of water to a gentle boil.
Using a spoon, lower your eggs in carefully, straight from the fridge, and start
your timer right away.
For a soft, jammy yolk with a just-set white, cook large eggs for six
to seven minutes.
For a creamy, almost-set yolk, go to eight minutes.
For a fully firm yolk, cook them for ten to eleven minutes.
Overcooking is what causes that grey-green ring around the yolk, so do not leave
the eggs in longer than you need to.
If you live somewhere high up, water boils at a lower temperature, so add
a minute or two to each timing.
When the timer goes off, move the eggs straight into the ice water for
five minutes.
This stops the cooking and makes them easier to peel.
To peel, tap the egg gently on the counter, roll it under your palm,
and start peeling at the wide end, where there is a small air pocket.
Very fresh eggs can be harder to peel, so eggs that are a week
or so old are a good choice.
Cooked eggs keep in the fridge for up to a week, so you can
make a batch and use them in salads, in sandwiches, or just with a
pinch of salt.
Those are the three timings to remember: six or seven minutes for jammy, eight
for creamy, and ten or eleven for firm.
If this helped, subscribe to the channel for more simple kitchen basics.
See you next time.
